## {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[🤖]{.lecture-icon}

### Today's question

**A model that reads your files, runs your code, opens a pull request.**

What is it made of, and how do we run it without losing the audit trail?

::: {.notes}
Audience: fluent in scientific computing, tired of the word "agent". Build from concept: context first, mechanism second, the four ways to use one, where it pays off, how to write your own, then GAIA. Say once, early, which words are one vendor's and which are general.
:::

## Sources

{{< include refs/agents-intro_refs.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Two blog posts from our own practice, the eScience half-day this mirrors, the vendor's own documentation for the surfaces, and one paper. Nothing on this deck is cited from memory; the amber blocks are what is still unverified.
:::

## Three words {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[0 to 3 min]{.minutes}

**Tool call**: the model writes, in a fixed format, "run this function with these arguments" instead of prose.

**Harness**: the program around the model that reads that request, runs the function, and hands the result back.

**Loop**: the harness doing that until the model stops asking.

::: {.takeaway}
That is all an agent is. The rest of the hour is detail.
:::

::: {.notes}
Define these before the timeline uses them; each gets a proper treatment in the next segment. Post-trained, when it comes up: trained after the main training, on tool use.
:::

## How we got here

![](../../../img/agents-timeline.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
Everyone has used the first dot: a chat box, 30 November 2022, GPT-3.5, text in and text out, no hands. March 2023: plugins, the model may ask for a function to be called; that is the conceptual step, the rest is training and engineering. November 2024: a standard for plugging tools in. February 2025: the vendor's first agentic coding tool, a research preview that reads code, edits files, runs tests, commits. And the window: 2,048 tokens on GPT-3, one million on the current models, enough for a repository and a day's transcript. Why not two years ago: in September 2024 the standard, the harnesses and the windows were all still to come; that reading of the dates is mine, not a source's.
:::

## Why it is useful now

- **Retrieval got good**: literature review is close to solved for a working scientist; models ground claims in real papers
- **Tool results are facts the model must read**: a failing test is in its window
- **The harness runs against your repository**: the unit of work is a pull request, not a pasted snippet

::: {.dim}
Denolle, Three Experiments in Agentic Research (June 2026).
:::

::: {.notes}
Three observations from practice, all from the June post. Hold the sceptic's "why an agent rather than a script" until the payoff segment: the answer is the spec.
:::

## Model, prompt, agent {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[3 to 8 min]{.minutes}

| | |
|---|---|
| **Open-weight model** | weights on your hardware; you pay in compute |
| **Private model** | API only; pay per token; can change under you |
| **Prompt** | text placed in the window. Nothing else happens. |
| **Agent** | the same model, in a loop, with tools |

::: {.notes}
Three definitions and one distinction. HazEvalHub's prototype ran a 7B Qwen and an 8B Llama locally next to cloud models. A prompt reads no file and runs no code; a chat interface hides this by re-sending the transcript. The agent is the model plus something that runs its commands.
:::

## Chat, script, agent

![](../../../img/agent-loop.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway}
Chat: you close every loop. Script: every branch pre-written. Agent: the model picks the next step from what it just saw.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk left to right. A: quality bounded by your patience for closing loops. B: deterministic; an unexpected input is a crash and a person reads the log. C: gather, act, verify, repeat. An unexpected state becomes a decision, which can be wrong or endless; a crash at least stops. The four verbs are our labels for what the tool calls turn out to be; the model has no stages, only one token stream. Next slide shows the whole thing as code.
:::

## The whole thing, mechanically

```python
messages = [system_prompt, context_file, tool_schemas, task]
while True:
    out = model(messages)                      # one API call: tokens in, tokens out
    if out.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break                                  # plain text: the model says it is done
    if not permitted(out.tool, out.args):      # the harness pauses here, not the model
        result = "denied by user"
    else:
        result = run(out.tool, out.args)       # shell, file, web, GitHub ...
    messages += [out, tool_result(result)]     # the result re-enters the window
```

::: {.dim}
Line 1: the harness's own standing text · the standing instructions in your repository · the functions the model may call, each with a name, description and argument schema · what you typed. A tool call is structured tokens the harness parses: `{"name": "bash", "input": {"command": "pixi run spellcheck"}}`. The harness is this loop plus the permission check. The loop is generic and the same under every vendor's product.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the debunk. The model is called once per turn with the whole message list and returns tokens. If they end in a structured tool-call block, the harness parses it, checks permissions, runs the function, appends the result, and calls the model again. No memory, no execution inside the model, no stages. Why a tool at all: next-token prediction cannot execute, count, or do arithmetic reliably; a shell with python in it is the workaround. A subagent is this loop started again with a fresh message list, launched by a tool call, whose final text comes back as a tool result. A permission prompt is the harness pausing between parse and run. The loop is only as good as its verify step, and it has no natural end: done, budget, or killed.
:::

## The pieces {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[8 to 14 min]{.minutes}

![](../../../img/agents-stack.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
One diagram, seven pieces. Left column is loaded every turn and paid for every call. Centre is the harness: the window and the loop. Right column is called on demand. Bottom is the model, which only ever sees tokens. Point at each box once; the next slides zoom in.

## Context file: ours

```
CLAUDE.md  →  5 lines, points at AGENTS.md
AGENTS.md  →  one screen: layout · build commands ·
              six conventions · persona reviews
```

::: {.takeaway}
What a good collaborator needs on day one and cannot find by reading the code. Nothing else.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show what it omits: no MyST tutorial, no restated CONTRIBUTING. The vendor docs say the harness reads CLAUDE.md and can read an AGENTS.md written for other agents. The March post: knowledge anchor, standing instructions, situated prompt; the first two set output quality; the instructions are a living document.
:::

## Skill · subagent · MCP {.smaller}

| | What it is | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | `SKILL.md`: description in the window from startup; the model picks it, the harness loads the body | `plain-voice`; one more built live today |
| **Subagent** | fresh window, own tools, one task; only the report returns | ten persona reviewers → `review-logs/` |
| **MCP** | open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems; "a USB-C port for AI applications" | tutorial 3 |

::: {.takeaway}
A skill costs its description on every call and its body only when loaded. Every MCP server you connect is a party whose output the model will act on.
:::

::: {.dim}
Vendor conventions: `CLAUDE.md`, skills, `claude -p`. General: the loop, `AGENTS.md` (the vendor's docs say it reads that too), subagents under some name in every harness, MCP as a published standard. Prompt injection: tool results and instructions are one token stream with no provenance bit; a sentence inside a fetched page reads like a sentence from you.
:::

::: {.notes}
The description is the part to keep short: re-sent on every call whether or not the skill fires; the body can be long. plain-voice: about 60 words of description, 2300 of body. Subagents buy a fresh window and attention per task, not fewer tokens. MCP definition and analogy are the protocol site's own words; the spec lives at modelcontextprotocol.io. Capability by configuration, risk by the same route.
:::

## Anatomy of one agent

![](../../../img/agents-anatomy.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
A real one: a persona reviewer from this repository. Left, the definition: front matter with a tools allow-list, then three files it reads at run time: who it is, how to run, how to judge. The rubric and method are shared, so ten personas score against one standard. Middle, the loop under a 30-minute timebox. Right, one structured file in review-logs, which a synthesis step merges. References and rubric are files, not prompts: that is what makes the output comparable across runs.
:::

## Orchestrator versus specialist

![](../../../img/agents-orchestrator-vs-specialist.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
The orchestrator holds a broad goal and only the ten reports; it dispatches, merges, and gates anything outward-facing. Each specialist holds the whole site for thirty minutes, with fixed weights and its own vocabulary, and writes one file. Isolation stops reviewers copying each other; it does not remove the weights they share, so treat convergence as a lead, not a statistic. If time is short, this slide or the previous one can go; tutorial 3 covers both.
:::

## The context window

![](../../../img/agents-context-window.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.dim}
Recall drops for material in the middle of a long context (Liu et al., 2024, TACL; on the sources slide). Compaction is itself a model call: the harness asks the model to summarise, then swaps the messages.
:::

::: {.notes}
Tool results are the part people forget. Compaction is a lossy summary; rules in the prompt may not survive it. Consequences: invariants in the context file, big reads in a subagent, new task in a new session. When a good agent drifts, suspect the window first.
:::

## Four ways to use one today {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[14 to 20 min]{.minutes}

![](../../../img/agents-four-ways.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
Surfaces from the vendor's documentation: terminal, VS Code and JetBrains, desktop app, web, one engine, one CLAUDE.md across all of them. The useful cut for this room: what can it touch, and who is watching. Browser chat cannot see your files or run your code; most beliefs about "AI coding" come from pasting snippets there. The app's Chat tab and Code tab are the same model without and with the loop: switching tabs is switching from panel A to panel C. The editor shows inline diffs; the CLI is the full surface, interactive or headless.
:::

## What each one can touch {.smaller}

| | Touches your repo | Who watches | Needs | Runs on a cluster over ssh |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Browser, Chat tab** | no | you, every turn | an account | n/a |
| **Browser, Code tab** | yes, in the cloud | you, per session | subscription | n/a |
| **App, Code tab** | yes | you, per diff; or nobody, if scheduled | subscription; download | no |
| **Editor** | yes | you, per line | subscription or key; extension | no |
| **CLI** `claude` / `-p` | yes | you, per gated action / nobody | subscription or key; one-line install | yes |

::: {.dim}
"Gated": a tool call the permission settings say must be approved first. Needs and installs from the vendor's overview page; monthly prices: TODO. Other vendors ship the same shapes (the lecturer's comparison names OpenAI's Codex); the names differ, the loop does not.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the table down "who watches": that is the real difference between rows. Two rows have "nobody" in them: headless CLI and scheduled app tasks; both need limits on turns, cost and wall clock. The cluster column is the HPC question: only the CLI is a plain terminal program.
:::

```
for issue in open_issues:

```

## Where it pays off for you {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[20 to 27 min]{.minutes}

![](../../../img/agents-payoff.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
The answer to "why an agent rather than a script". A script when you know every step; an agent when you can state what done looks like but not how to get there, and getting there is mostly typing you have done before. Five uses in project order: you write the spec; the agent works to it; you look at the raw data.
:::

## 1. Write the spec first

```
# SPEC: <name>
Purpose: one sentence.
Inputs: files, formats, units, coordinate frames.
Outputs: files, formats, units; what a plot of them should look like.
Conventions: package layout, style, test runner, the CI that must stay green.
Done when: tests/test_<name>.py passes; the figure in docs/ shows <what>.
Out of scope: what not to touch.
```

::: {.takeaway}
Draft it with the agent, edit it yourself. The spec is the contract; everything after is checked against it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Agent errors are specification and judgement errors. A good spec removes the first kind and makes the second visible. Then: intent, not syntax: "implement section 3; stop when the first test passes" rather than "write a function that opens the file".
:::

## 2 to 4. Intent, template, tests

```
"Write the tests for module X from SPEC.md and run them. Do not change X
 to make a test pass; if a test is right and X is wrong, fix X and say so."

"Implement section 3 of SPEC.md; stop when tests/test_io.py passes."

"Set up a Python repository for X using pixi and best current standards:
 pyproject, one passing test, CI that runs it, README, licence, .gitignore."
```

::: {.takeaway}
Tests from the spec first, then implement to them. State the goal and the stop condition; the agent picks the steps. Check the template against the list.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three prompt shapes. The repository template is an afternoon of boilerplate the agent does in minutes, and the CSSI plan's gaia-template-agent is this use made reusable. The tests-first use is the one the vendor's own documentation puts first. The last line of the third prompt is the minimal-change rule in another form.
:::

## 5. Show me the raw data

```
"At every stage of the pipeline, save a figure of the raw waveforms and of
 the intermediate arrays, and the first and last rows of every table, to
 docs/figures/, and list them in the README."
```

::: {.takeaway}
Tests written by the same agent inherit its reading of the spec; the raw data do not. If they look wrong, the pipeline is wrong, whatever the tests say.
:::

::: {.notes}
The one use on the list that is specific to science, and the one the room should leave with. It is also the cheapest guardrail we have.
:::

## Live: a real act and a real verify

**Before the talk:** a scratch page under `book/teaching/` with one misspelling. Not committed.

**Ask:** the spellcheck fails; fix it and show me it passes.

**Watch:** `pixi run spellcheck` → read the page → edit one word → rerun → exit 0

::: {.takeaway}
The pass condition is the repository's own check, not the model's opinion. More than one word edited is the minimal-change rule in `AGENTS.md` broken in front of you.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, rehearsed. Narrate each call as it appears. If the agent reruns the check on its own, point at it: that is the verify step nobody told it to do. Delete the scratch page afterwards; a committed misspelling fails CI.
:::

## Writing your own {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[27 to 33 min]{.minutes}

| | You write | Choose it when | Start from |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A skill** | a `SKILL.md` | this session should follow a procedure, in its own window | `.claude/skills/plain-voice` |
| **An agent definition** | a Markdown file: role, tools, instructions | the task needs a fresh window, fewer tools, or parallel copies | `.claude/agents/gaia-review-*.md` |
| **A loop in Python** | tools as functions | the model or the harness is not the vendor's (tutorial 4's local model) | twelve lines, two slides on |

::: {.notes}
Three ways, in increasing order of how much you own. The first two are files in this repository; copy one and change it. The third is for a model or a harness the vendor's product does not run.
:::

## Live: the skill

```
.claude/skills/nsf-acknowledgement/SKILL.md
---
name: nsf-acknowledgement
description: Insert the agreed GAIA acknowledgement wording for the NSF
  awards, verbatim, when a page, talk, poster or paper needs a funding
  statement.
---
1. Read the wording from book/governance/how-we-work.md. Never embed it here.
2. Insert it verbatim, all three award numbers included.
3. If the seed grant or the Paros Center contributed, append the page's
   second sentence.
```

::: {.dim}
An agent definition has the same front matter plus a `tools:` line, then instructions: `name: gaia-review-phd-student-prospective` · `tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Type it live. Then the flow on the next slide: fresh session, ask for a funding acknowledgement on mt-rainier.md, watch whether it triggers; if not, fix the description in front of the room. Loading a skill is itself a tool call, but it adds no capability: it can only use the tools the agent already has.
:::

## How the skill runs

![](../../../img/agents-skill-flow.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
The problem: the governance page requires the NSF acknowledgement verbatim; an agent will paraphrase. The model picks the skill from its description; the harness loads the body; the body reads the page at use time so there is one source of truth. Tradeoff to name: longer descriptions fire more reliably and cost more per call.
:::

## The loop in twelve real lines

```python
import subprocess, anthropic
from anthropic import beta_tool

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

@beta_tool
def spellcheck(path: str) -> str:
    """Run the repository spellcheck on one file and return its output."""
    r = subprocess.run(["codespell", path], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return r.stdout or "clean"

runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=[spellcheck],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Fix the misspelling in docs/demo.md."}],
)
for message in runner:   # one iteration per model turn; stops when no tool is called
    print(message)
```

::: {.dim}
Shape from the vendor SDK reference. Underneath: `messages.create`, check `stop_reason`, run each `tool_use`, append a `tool_result` with the block's id, repeat: the code slide from minute 5 with real names. Batteries-included harness as a library: the Agent SDK.
:::

::: {.todo}
Verify against the installed SDK version before showing; add the Agent SDK link from a fetched page.
:::

::: {.notes}
A tool is a decorated function with a docstring; the runner drives the loop and stops when the model makes no tool call. This is the whole of "writing an agent" for anything the harness does not already do. Other vendors have equivalents.
:::

## How we score an agent

![](../../../img/agents-evaluation.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway}
Three questions per submission, a hidden test split, cost on the axis. The board is live for agent tasks; dashed boxes are the CSSI plan, years one to three.
:::

::: {.notes}
A CSSI deliverable, not an aside. Task with a hidden test split; four conditions: local or cloud, with or without skills; the harness runs it in its container against a declarative JSON scoring spec and emits a scorecard: right, cost, reproducible, plus provenance. Consumers: the board, where the line between hollow and filled is the skill lift; a CI regression gate; the Metrics Observatory. The expert track answers whether the answer is useful, not how the model behaves. Tutorial 4 is a miniature of this diagram.
:::

## Guardrails, trajectory, cost, reproducibility {background-color="#f5f3fb"}

[39 to 45 min]{.minutes}

![](../../../img/agents-trajectory.svg){.r-stretch}

::: {.notes}
Guardrails: three from the coordination plan, two from practice. The trajectory is the record we owe every reader; HazEvalHub already scores three questions per submission and names trajectory scoring. The amber box is the open question: four capture candidates, none verified. The decision is the group's: default mechanism, storage, who may read.
:::

## Why two runs differ

- **Sampling**: the next token is drawn, not argmaxed; the API used here exposes no seed and, on current models, no sampling parameters at all
- **Batched inference**: generally not bit-reproducible on shared accelerators (TODO: cite)
- **Model updates**: the same name can point at new weights; pin the version string
- **Tool results**: the web, the data, and the repo moved between runs

::: {.takeaway}
Reproducibility of an agent run is statistical. Report N, pin versions, keep every tool result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Tutorial 4 scores reproducibility as the fraction of identical outputs across N runs. These four are what makes that fraction less than one. The first two are properties of the model service; the last two are properties of the world the agent touched, and only the trajectory records them.
:::

## Cost

::: {.big-number}
~$200 / month [one person, one project, the coding agent; no model or run count given. Denolle (June 2026)]{.unit}
:::

::: {.dim}
Scale: the vendor's current models cost 1 to 10 dollars per million input tokens and 5 to 50 per million output (models page, 21 Sep 2026).
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Cost is a first-class axis: recorded per run, reported next to accuracy. On the FrugalMind board, local 7B models with skills scored perfectly on configuration tasks and failed numerical code, where cloud models went from about 0.56 to 0.76 with skills. Task counts and N: TODO.
:::

::: {.notes}
One fact from practice, one from the eval board. The skill-lift result is why open-weight models stay in the comparison. Tutorial costs are TODO in the compute-requirements document.
:::

## Reproducibility

- If an agent cannot reproduce your work, neither can your collaborators (Denolle, June 2026)
- A **Reproducibility Statement** in every paper, beside data availability
- The coordination plan already requires a provenance YAML and an RO-Crate per agent and publication

::: {.takeaway}
The missing link is the trajectory inside the provenance record. Tutorial 4 builds toward it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Close the arc where it started: the loop leaves a trace, and the trace is what we owe every reader.
:::
